newsitem.title: UK: Police chief says his force main IRA target.
newsitem.headline: Police chief says his force main IRA target.

text.p: Northern Ireland's police chief said on Sunday that IRA guerrillas appeared determined to kill members of his force in a rapdily escalating 1997 campaign which has raised fears of a return to total sectarian warfare.

Ronnie Flanagan, Chief Constable of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police, said "at this stage of the campaign it is directed principally against our officers and against the military colleagues who support us".

He was speaking 12 hours after two police officers and a woman motorist had a narrow escape when two horizontal mortars were fired at a police patrol near Downpatrick, 30 miles (50 km) southeast of Belfast.

No-one has claimed responsibility for the attack, but it had all the hallmarks of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland to reunite it with the Irish republic.
Police said the mortars were fired at a patrol answering an emergency call. The mortars passed over their armoured jeep and the car of the motorist coming from the opposite direction.
The latest violence prompted Roman Catholic Archbishop Sean Brady to urge the IRA to seek a negotiated settlement for peace in Northern Ireland.
"I think it takes great courage to negotiate, probably more courage than maybe to do acts of violence. I would appeal to people to think about that," he said.
"The only way forward is through dialogue and negotiation and it will have to come some day."
Assistant Chief Constable Freddy Hall said:"This was not only a murderous attack on the police but a murderous attack on the motoring public. It is a miracle no one was killed or seriously injured."

Flanagan told Sir David Frost's Sunday morning television programme:"There are no grounds whatsoever for any violence. None of these attacks further any ends. There is no public or popular support for it what so ever,"

The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year by bombing targets in Britain and a British army base in Germany in protest at the failure of its political wing, Sinn Fein, to win a seat at multi-party peace talks in Belfast.
No-one has been killed in Northern Ireland since the IRA returned to war in the province itself by bombing Britain's army base outside Belfast last October, killing one soldier.

But security forces fear that it is only a matter of time before the IRA kills a member of the 18,000-strong force and forces its Protestant Loyalist adversaries to end a two-year truce and return to tit-for-tat revenge violence.
The Ulster Freedom Fighters, one outlawed Loyalist group, said last month that it would end its truce if the IRA killed anyone and police say they are taking the threat seriously.
Loyalists, who want Northern Ireland to remain British, called a truce in October 1994.

If they ended the truce and returned to their pattern of killing members of the Catholic community from which the IRA draws support, it would increase pressure for the expulsion of their political spokesmen from the Belfast peace talks.

Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, is excluded from the negotiations until the IRA calls a permanent halt to violence but the guerrillas say that Sinn Fein should be invited to the negotiations without any preconditions.
